questions.stem: A woman with a mitochondrial myopathy has several children with very different severity. Her brother, also affected, has unaffected children. What explains both observations?

options.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance

questions.explanation: mtDNA passes only through mothers; heteroplasmy (via the bottleneck) gives variable severity. B: Affected X-linked males would pass it to daughters. C: AD would allow paternal transmission. D: Imprinting depends on parent of origin of a nuclear gene. E: Anticipation needs repeat expansion.
questions.source: Unusual Patterns of Inheritance, slides 7; reading p9–10

questions.stem: A 15q11–13 deletion is found in a child with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, ataxia, seizures, and frequent laughter. On which parental chromosome is the deletion?

options.D: Paternal; UBE3A is expressed only from the paternal copy in brain

questions.explanation: Angelman results from loss of maternal UBE3A expression (maternal deletion in ~70%, paternal UPD, or UBE3A mutation). A: A paternal deletion causes Prader-Willi. B: This region is imprinted. C: A homozygous deletion isn't the mechanism. D: UBE3A is paternally imprinted (silenced) in brain, so the maternal copy is the expressed one.
questions.source: Unusual Patterns of Inheritance, slide 30; reading p8

questions.stem: A hypotonic newborn later develops hyperphagia, obesity, and hypogonadism. FISH for 15q11–13 is normal, but methylation testing is abnormal. What is the most likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: Prader-Willi without a deletion is almost always maternal UPD15 (no paternal copy). A: Paternal UPD15 causes Angelman. B: UBE3A mutations cause Angelman. D: A deletion would show on FISH. E: A maternal deletion causes Angelman and would also show on FISH.
questions.source: Unusual Patterns of Inheritance, slide 30; reading p8

questions.stem: A young man has intellectual disability, a long face, large ears, and macroorchidism. What is the molecular basis?

options.A: CAG expansion in the coding region of huntingtin
options.B: CGG expansion in the FMR1 5′ UTR with methylation and silencing
options.C: CTG expansion in the DMPK 3′ UTR

questions.explanation: Fragile X: a full CGG expansion in the FMR1 5′ UTR (>250 repeats per the slide) is methylated, so FMRP is absent. A: Huntington disease. C: Myotonic dystrophy. D: Friedreich ataxia. E: Prader-Willi/Angelman.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has premature ovarian failure. Her nephew has fragile X syndrome. What is her most likely genotype?

options.E: Skewed X inactivation of a normal X

questions.explanation: Premutation carriers (59 to ~200 CGG repeats) have a ~20% risk of premature ovarian failure before 40; full-mutation carriers don't. A: Full mutations aren't linked to ovarian failure. B: A normal allele wouldn't explain it. C: UPD of X isn't the mechanism. E: Skewing of a normal X doesn't cause ovarian failure.

questions.stem: Which mtDNA defect is typical of Kearns-Sayre syndrome?
questions.explanation: KSS, Pearson syndrome, and CPEO are caused by single mtDNA deletions. A: MELAS. B: MERRF. C: LHON. D: POLG causes SANDO/MIRAS.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has diabetes and progressive bilateral hearing loss; her mother had the same, and her brother has recurrent stroke-like episodes with lactic acidosis. Which variant is most likely?
questions.explanation: m.3243A>G most often presents as maternally inherited diabetes and deafness, and also causes MELAS. B: MERRF (myoclonus, ragged red fibers). C: NARP. D: LHON. E: Fragile X–associated disorders.

questions.stem: A complete hydatidiform mole has a 46,XX karyotype. What is the parental origin of its genome?

options.C: Maternal with one extra paternal set
options.E: Paternal with one extra maternal set

questions.explanation: Complete moles are androgenetic, so paternal genome leads to placental overgrowth with no fetus. A: Entirely maternal is an ovarian teratoma. B: That's normal. C: That's a partial mole (69,XXY). E: A maternal extra set gives a small placenta.
questions.source: Unusual Patterns of Inheritance, reading p8

questions.stem: A man inherited from his mother an allele that is silenced by maternal imprinting in his somatic cells. What imprint will this allele carry in his sperm?

options.B: Paternal imprint, after erasure and resetting
options.D: Maternal imprint in half of his sperm
options.E: A random imprint set at fertilization

questions.explanation: Imprints are maintained through somatic divisions but erased and reset during gametogenesis, so all of a man's gametes carry a paternal imprint. A: Maintenance applies to somatic cells, not gametes. C: The imprint is reset, not lost. D: Gametes are 100% maternal or 100% paternal by the parent's sex. E: Imprints are set during gametogenesis, before fertilization.
